claim: The liver, specifically hepatocytes, are widely accepted as the main source of hepatitis C virus (HCV) production.
source: While the liver, specifically hepatocytes, are widely accepted as the main source of hepatitis C virus (HCV) production, the role of the liver/hepatocytes in clearance of circulating HCV remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific consensus in the abstract and introduction.

claim: The role of the liver/hepatocytes in clearance of circulating HCV remains unknown.
source: While the liver, specifically hepatocytes, are widely accepted as the main source of hepatitis C virus (HCV) production, the role of the liver/hepatocytes in clearance of circulating HCV remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the abstract.

claim: Frequent HCV kinetic data were recorded from five liver transplant patients throughout the anhepatic phase and for 4 hr post-reperfusion.
source: Frequent HCV kinetic data were recorded and mathematically modeled from five liver transplant patients throughout the anhepatic (absence of liver) phase and for 4 hr post-reperfusion.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and data collection performed in the study.

claim: During the anhepatic phase, HCV remained at pre-anhepatic levels in three patients.
source: During the anhepatic phase, HCV remained at pre-anhepatic levels (n = 3) or declined (n = 2) with t1/2~1 hr.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the patient data presented in the study.

claim: During the anhepatic phase, HCV declined in two patients with t1/2~1 hr.
source: During the anhepatic phase, HCV remained at pre-anhepatic levels (n = 3) or declined (n = 2) with t1/2~1 hr.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the patient data presented in the study.

claim: Immediately post-reperfusion, virus declined in a biphasic manner in four patients consisting of a rapid decline (t1/2 = 5 min) followed by a slower decline (t1/2 = 67 min).
source: Immediately post-reperfusion, virus declined in a biphasic manner in four patients consisting of a rapid decline (t1/2 = 5 min) followed by a slower decline (t1/2 = 67 min).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the patient data and mathematical modeling presented in the study.

claim: The HCV t1/2 in cell culture was longer in the absence of chronically HCV-infected cells compared to their presence.
source: Consistent with the majority of patients in the anhepatic phase, when we monitored HCV clearance at 37°C from culture medium in the absence/presence of chronically infected hepatoma cells that were inhibited from secreting HCV, the HCV t1/2 in cell culture was longer in the absence of chronically HCV-infected cells.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the in vitro experiments described in the study.

claim: The liver plays a major role in the clearance of circulating HCV.
source: The results suggest that the liver plays a major role in the clearance of circulating HCV and that hepatocytes may be involved.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the in vivo patient data showing viral plateau during anhepatic phase.

claim: Hepatocytes may be involved in the clearance of circulating HCV.
source: The results suggest that the liver plays a major role in the clearance of circulating HCV and that hepatocytes may be involved.
evidence: This is inferred from both in vivo and in vitro data showing faster HCV clearance in the presence of hepatocytes.

claim: Previous kinetic studies suggested that HCV was cleared at the same rate during the anhepatic phase and early after reperfusion.
source: Previous kinetic studies (Dahari et al., 2005; Fukumoto et al., 1996; Garcia-Retortillo et al., 2002; Hughes et al., 2017; Powers et al., 2006) have suggested that HCV was cleared at the same rate during the anhepatic phase and early after reperfusion.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous estimates of HCV clearance rates were based on limited data (one to four samples during the anhepatic phase).
source: However, these estimates were based on limited data (one to four samples during the anhepatic phase), obtained at the beginning and end of the anhepatic phase and several hours after reperfusion.
evidence: This is a critique of previous studies based on their methodology.

claim: Garcia-Retortillo et al., 2002, reported a patient with a prolonged anhepatic phase of 20 hr in whom the HCV half-life during the anhepatic phase was estimated to be 10.3 hr.
source: Interestingly, Garcia-Retortillo et al., 2002, reported a patient with a prolonged anhepatic phase of 20 hr in whom the HCV half-live (t1/2) during the anhepatic phase and after reperfusion was estimated to be 10.3 and 3.8 hr, respectively, suggesting that viral clearance occurs relatively slowly during the anhepatic phase and increases after reperfusion.
evidence: This is a specific finding from a cited previous study.

claim: Garcia-Retortillo et al., 2002, reported a patient with a prolonged anhepatic phase of 20 hr in whom the HCV half-life after reperfusion was estimated to be 3.8 hr.
source: Interestingly, Garcia-Retortillo et al., 2002, reported a patient with a prolonged anhepatic phase of 20 hr in whom the HCV half-live (t1/2) during the anhepatic phase and after reperfusion was estimated to be 10.3 and 3.8 hr, respectively, suggesting that viral clearance occurs relatively slowly during the anhepatic phase and increases after reperfusion.
evidence: This is a specific finding from a cited previous study.

claim: Garcia-Retortillo et al., 2002, hypothesized that the rapid clearance of HCV from the serum post-reperfusion was at least in part due to entrance of HCV into the hepatocytes or the liver reticuloendothelial system.
source: Garcia-Retortillo et al., 2002, also hypothesized that the rapid clearance of HCV from the serum post-reperfusion was at least in part due to entrance of HCV into the hepatocytes or the liver reticuloendothelial system.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from a cited previous study.

claim: A detailed viral kinetic study during the anhepatic phase and immediately after reperfusion has not been performed prior to this study.
source: However, a detailed viral kinetic study during the anhepatic phase and immediately after reperfusion has not been performed.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Viral levels were measured in five liver transplant patients over the course of liver transplantation.
source: Here, we measured viral levels in five liver transplant patients over the course of liver transplantation (Figure 1a).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study with reference to Figure 1a.

claim: Very frequent sampling was performed during the anhepatic phase (every 5–15 min).
source: We focus on very frequent sampling during the anhepatic phase (i.e., every 5–15 min) and during the first 4 hr of the reperfusion period (every 5–10 min) (Figure 1b) along with recording fluid balances during the surgical procedure (Table 1).
evidence: This describes the sampling frequency used in the study.

claim: Very frequent sampling was performed during the first 4 hr of the reperfusion period (every 5–10 min).
source: We focus on very frequent sampling during the anhepatic phase (i.e., every 5–15 min) and during the first 4 hr of the reperfusion period (every 5–10 min) (Figure 1b) along with recording fluid balances during the surgical procedure (Table 1).
evidence: This describes the sampling frequency used in the study.

claim: Fluid balances during the surgical procedure were recorded.
source: We focus on very frequent sampling during the anhepatic phase (i.e., every 5–15 min) and during the first 4 hr of the reperfusion period (every 5–10 min) (Figure 1b) along with recording fluid balances during the surgical procedure (Table 1).
evidence: This describes data collection during the study.

claim: The viral clearance rate during the anhepatic and reperfusion phases was estimated using a mathematical modeling framework accounting for viral kinetics and fluid balance.
source: The viral clearance rate during these two distinct phases was estimated using a mathematical modeling framework (Figure 2) accounting for viral kinetics and taking into account fluid balance including infusion of red blood cells, plasma, saline, and albumin, as well as blood loss.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach used in the study.

claim: HCV serum levels were observed to remain at steady state during the anhepatic phase in three of the five patients.
source: HCV serum levels were observed to remain at steady state during the AH phase in three of the five patients suggesting that the liver plays a major role in clearing HCV from the circulation.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the patient data.

claim: HCV clearance was faster in the presence of chronically infected hepatoma cells compared to the absence of cells in vitro.
source: Interestingly, in parallel in vitro experiments, when we monitored the clearance rate of HCV from culture medium at 37°C in the absence and presence of chronically infected Huh7 human hepatoma cells, HCV clearance was faster in the presence of the hepatoma cells suggesting that hepatocytes may play a role in the observed clearance of circulating HCV.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the in vitro experiments.

claim: In all patients, virus levels decreased after graft reperfusion.
source: In all patients, virus levels decreased after graft reperfusion.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 caption and describes a general observation across all patients.

claim: A nadir in viral levels was reached after a median time of 15 hr (range 9–87 hr) post-reperfusion.
source: A nadir was reached after a median time of 15 hr (range 9–87 hr) post-reperfusion.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the patient data described in Figure 1 caption.

claim: HCV RNA resurged within 7 days after reperfusion in all five cases.
source: HCV RNA resurged within 7 days after reperfusion, with three of five cases reaching greater or comparable viral levels to those observed at baseline.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the patient data described in Figure 1 caption.

claim: Three of five cases reached greater or comparable viral levels to baseline within 7 days after reperfusion.
source: HCV RNA resurged within 7 days after reperfusion, with three of five cases reaching greater or comparable viral levels to those observed at baseline.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the patient data described in Figure 1 caption.

claim: For two cases, the viral loads 7 days post-reperfusion were 0.87 and 0.43 log10 IU/mL lower than those just before surgery.
source: For the remaining two cases, the corresponding viral loads were 0.87 and 0.43 log10 IU/mL lower than those just before surgery.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the patient data described in Figure 1 caption.

claim: HCV RNA levels in Case 5 remained in a lower plateau from 11 hr post-surgery until the end of follow-up period with a corresponding viral load of 2.45 ± 0.002 log10 IU/mL.
source: HCV RNA levels in Case 5 remained in a lower plateau from 11 hr post-surgery until the end of follow-up period (slope <0.001, p = 0.76), with a corresponding viral load of 2.45 ± 0.002 log10 IU/mL.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the patient data described in Figure 1 caption.

claim: Prior to the anhepatic phase, viral load is at a steady state in which virus production is balanced by viral clearance.
source: Prior to the anhepatic (AH) phase viral load is at a steady state in which virus production is balanced by viral clearance (Equation 1).
evidence: This is a modeling assumption stated in Figure 2 caption.

claim: During the anhepatic phase, the liver is not present and therefore there is no viral production.
source: During the AH phase, the liver is not present and therefore there is no viral production (Equation 2).
evidence: This is a modeling assumption stated in Figure 2 caption based on the biological situation.

claim: During the anhepatic phase, virus may appear to be cleared by the input of fluids that dilute the virus in circulation.
source: However, virus may appear to be cleared by the input of fluids that dilute the virus in circulation (see F in Equation 3) and through processes of physiological clearance.
evidence: This is a modeling consideration stated in Figure 2 caption.

claim: Up to 4 hr post-reperfusion there is no viral production as the cells in the new liver if they have been infected have not yet started releasing new virions.
source: Up to 4 hr post-reperfusion there is no viral production as the cells in the new liver if they have been infected have not yet started releasing new virions.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption stated in Figure 2 caption based on biological reasoning.

claim: Longer after reperfusion (over 4 hr), the new liver begins producing new virions in Cases 1–4.
source: Longer after reperfusion (over 4 hr), the new liver begins producing new virions (as evident in Figure 1a in Cases 1–4).
evidence: This is inferred from the viral resurgence observed in Figure 1a.

claim: The median viral load measured just before the anhepatic phase was 6.0 (range 3.7–6.4) log10 IU/mL.
source: The median viral load measured just before the anhepatic phase was 6.0 (range 3.7–6.4) log10 IU/mL (Figure 3; Table 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the patient data.

claim: The anhepatic phase lasted 1.25–1.90 hr.
source: We carried out a linear fit to the data during the anhepatic phase, which lasted 1.25–1.90 hr.
evidence: This is a measurement of the surgical procedure duration.

claim: Virus levels were flat in Case 1, Case 2, and Case 3 during the anhepatic phase.
source: We found that virus levels were flat in three cases (Case 1, Case 2, and Case 3) while in two patients (Case 4 and Case 5) the viral decline slope was 0.32 and 0.16 log10 IU/mL per hour, respectively (Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the patient data analysis.

claim: In Case 4, the viral decline slope during the anhepatic phase was 0.32 log10 IU/mL per hour.
source: We found that virus levels were flat in three cases (Case 1, Case 2, and Case 3) while in two patients (Case 4 and Case 5) the viral decline slope was 0.32 and 0.16 log10 IU/mL per hour, respectively (Table 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the patient data analysis.

claim: In Case 5, the viral decline slope during the anhepatic phase was 0.16 log10 IU/mL per hour.
source: We found that virus levels were flat in three cases (Case 1, Case 2, and Case 3) while in two patients (Case 4 and Case 5) the viral decline slope was 0.32 and 0.16 log10 IU/mL per hour, respectively (Table 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the patient data analysis.

claim: Fluid input during post-reperfusion for Cases 1–5 were 0, 1000, 250, 3300, and 3350 mL, respectively.
source: Fluid input during post-reperfusion for Cases 1–5 were 0, 1000, 250, 3300, and 3350 mL, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the surgical procedure records.

claim: In Cases 1–4, HCV RNA declined in a biphasic manner during the first 4 hr after reperfusion.
source: In Cases 1–4, HCV RNA declined in a biphasic manner, while in Case 5, HCV RNA remained at the same levels as at the end of the anhepatic phase.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the patient data.

claim: In Case 5, HCV RNA remained at the same levels as at the end of the anhepatic phase during the first 4 hr after reperfusion.
source: In Cases 1–4, HCV RNA declined in a biphasic manner, while in Case 5, HCV RNA remained at the same levels as at the end of the anhepatic phase.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the patient data.

claim: For Cases 1–4, the biphasic decline consisted of an initial, sharp decrease within 11–22 min, followed by a longer but slower decrease.
source: For Cases 1–4, the biphasic decline consisted of an initial, sharp decrease within 11–22 min, followed by a longer but slower decrease (Table 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the patient data analysis.

claim: The slope of the initial decrease was 2.7, 1.5, 2.1, and 2.0 log10 IU/mL per hour for Cases 1–4, respectively.
source: Using linear regression, the slope of the initial decrease was 2.7, 1.5, 2.1, and 2.0 log10 IU/mL per hour for Cases 1–4, respectively, that lasted for 1.2–2.8 min.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from linear regression analysis of patient data.

claim: The initial decrease lasted for 1.2–2.8 min in Cases 1–4.
source: Using linear regression, the slope of the initial decrease was 2.7, 1.5, 2.1, and 2.0 log10 IU/mL per hour for Cases 1–4, respectively, that lasted for 1.2–2.8 min.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the patient data analysis.

claim: The slower second phase slope for Cases 1–4 was 0.2, 0.3, 0.2, and 0.4 log10 IU/mL per hour, respectively.
source: The slower second phase slope for Cases 1–4 was 0.2, 0.3, 0.2, and 0.4 log10 IU/mL per hour, respectively (Table 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from linear regression analysis of patient data.

claim: Case 5's viral load continued to be flat for ~6 days post-reperfusion.
source: The viral plateau in Case 5 is distinct from the other cases, although it is worth noting that this patient's viral load continued to be flat for ~6 days post-reperfusion (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the patient data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The estimated virus clearance rates during the anhepatic phase in Cases 1–3 were ~0 (i.e., very long t1/2 that implies no clearance).
source: The estimated virus clearance rates during the anhepatic phase in Cases 1–3 were ~0 (i.e., very long t1/2 that implies no clearance) but were significantly different from 0 in Cases 4 and 5 corresponding to an HCV t1/2 = Ln(2)/cAH of 1–2 hr.
evidence: This is a result from mathematical modeling of the patient data.

claim: The estimated virus clearance rates during the anhepatic phase in Cases 4 and 5 were significantly different from 0, corresponding to an HCV t1/2 of 1–2 hr.
source: The estimated virus clearance rates during the anhepatic phase in Cases 1–3 were ~0 (i.e., very long t1/2 that implies no clearance) but were significantly different from 0 in Cases 4 and 5 corresponding to an HCV t1/2 = Ln(2)/cAH of 1–2 hr.
evidence: This is a result from mathematical modeling of the patient data.

claim: For Cases 1–4, the initial viral clearance, c0, gave t1/2 on the order of 5 [0.4–16] min.
source: For Cases 1–4, the initial viral clearance, c0, gave t1/2 on the order of 5 [0.4–16] min (Table 5).
evidence: This is a result from mathematical modeling of the patient data.

claim: The median time constant was κ = 399/day meaning that the time it took for the clearance rate to shift from its initial value of c0 to its final value of cRP was around 4 min.
source: The median time constant was κ = 399/day meaning that the time it took for the clearance rate to shift from its initial value of c0 to its final value of cRP was around 4 min.
evidence: This is a result from mathematical modeling of the patient data.

claim: The second, slower clearance rate, cRP, corresponded to a t1/2 of order 67 [54–79] min.
source: The second, slower clearance rate, cRP, corresponded to a t1/2 of order 67 [54–79] min (Table 5 and Figure 3).
evidence: This is a result from mathematical modeling of the patient data.

claim: In Case 5, an extremely slow viral decline was observed during the first 4 hr post-reperfusion (slope of 0.06 log10 IU/mL/hr).
source: In Case 5, Equation. (3) was used because an extremely slow (or plateaued) viral load (slope of 0.06 log10 IU/mL/hr) was observed suggesting no production and clearance during the first 6 hr post-reperfusion (Figure 3, Table 5) or the subsequent 6 days (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the patient data analysis.

claim: In the absence of cells, the HCV half-life observed in vitro was 112 hr.
source: In the absence of cells, the HCV half-life observed was 112 hr (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the in vitro experiments.

claim: In the presence of chronically infected cells inhibited from de novo virus secretion, the HCV half-life observed in vitro was 13 hr.
source: In the presence of chronically infected cells inhibited from de novo virus secretion, the HCV half-life observed was 13 hr (Figure 4b), which is 8.5 times faster than the clearance observed in the absence of cells (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the in vitro experiments.

claim: HCV clearance in the presence of chronically infected cells is 8.5 times faster than in the absence of cells in vitro.
source: In the presence of chronically infected cells inhibited from de novo virus secretion, the HCV half-life observed was 13 hr (Figure 4b), which is 8.5 times faster than the clearance observed in the absence of cells (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of the in vitro experimental results.

claim: The current study employs in vivo clinical methods and mathematical modeling to assess virus levels during the anhepatic phase and immediately after graft reperfusion.
source: The current cross-disciplinary study employs in vivo clinical methods and mathematical modeling to assess virus levels during the anhepatic phase and immediately after graft reperfusion, providing evidence that the liver plays a major role in HCV clearance from the circulation.
evidence: This describes the methodology of the current study.

claim: The current study provides evidence that the liver plays a major role in HCV clearance from the circulation.
source: The current cross-disciplinary study employs in vivo clinical methods and mathematical modeling to assess virus levels during the anhepatic phase and immediately after graft reperfusion, providing evidence that the liver plays a major role in HCV clearance from the circulation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the data and modeling.

claim: Liver sinusoidal endothelial cells may be responsible for clearance of other viruses from circulation.
source: While others have suggested that the liver sinusoidal endothelial may be responsible for clearance of other viruses from circulation (Ganesan et al., 2011), our in vitro data also implicates hepatocytes as possibly playing a role, opening up a new avenue for investigation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The in vitro data implicates hepatocytes as possibly playing a role in HCV clearance.
source: While others have suggested that the liver sinusoidal endothelial may be responsible for clearance of other viruses from circulation (Ganesan et al., 2011), our in vitro data also implicates hepatocytes as possibly playing a role, opening up a new avenue for investigation.
evidence: This is inferred from the in vitro experimental results.

claim: Viral clearance is often minimal during the anhepatic phase.
source: This frequent sampling revealed that viral clearance is often minimal during the anhepatic phase, which goes against our and others' assumptions in previous models in which similar viral clearance rates were assumed during both the anhepatic and post-reperfusion phases (Dahari et al., 2005; Garcia-Retortillo et al., 2002; Hughes et al., 2017; Powers et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the patient data analysis.

claim: Previous models assumed similar viral clearance rates during both the anhepatic and post-reperfusion phases.
source: This frequent sampling revealed that viral clearance is often minimal during the anhepatic phase, which goes against our and others' assumptions in previous models in which similar viral clearance rates were assumed during both the anhepatic and post-reperfusion phases (Dahari et al., 2005; Garcia-Retortillo et al., 2002; Hughes et al., 2017; Powers et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In three of five cases, viral load remained at a plateau in the absence of the liver indicating that not only viral production stopped but that viral clearance stopped as well.
source: Specifically, in three of five cases, viral load remained at a plateau in the absence of the liver indicating that not only viral production stopped but that viral clearance stopped as well, suggesting that the liver is involved in the clearance of circulating HCV.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the patient data.

claim: In Cases 4 and 5, fast viral clearance (t1/2~1–2 hr) was estimated during the anhepatic phase while accounting for the recorded high fluid input.
source: Interestingly, however, in Cases 4 and 5, fast viral clearance (t1/2~1–2 hr) was estimated via model calibration with measured data during the anhepatic phase while accounting for the recorded high fluid input of 3300 and 3350 mL in Cases 4 and 5, respectively (Equation. 3).
evidence: This is a result from mathematical modeling of the patient data.

claim: To explain the fast viral clearance in Cases 4 and 5 solely based on fluid input, the model predicts about fourfold higher fluid input (~13,000 mL) than the recorded input.
source: Theoretically, to explain the fast viral clearance solely based on fluid input, the model (Equation. 3) predicts about fourfold higher fluid input (i.e, ~13,000 mL) than the recorded input (not shown), suggesting that other extrahepatic mechanisms must have contributed to viral clearance during the anhepatic phase in these patients.
evidence: This is a result from mathematical modeling analysis.

claim: Other extrahepatic mechanisms must have contributed to viral clearance during the anhepatic phase in Cases 4 and 5.
source: Theoretically, to explain the fast viral clearance solely based on fluid input, the model (Equation. 3) predicts about fourfold higher fluid input (i.e, ~13,000 mL) than the recorded input (not shown), suggesting that other extrahepatic mechanisms must have contributed to viral clearance during the anhepatic phase in these patients.
evidence: This is inferred from the discrepancy between model predictions and recorded data.

claim: The current study includes five patients who underwent liver transplant before the era of direct-acting antivirals (DAA) and were viremic at the time of transplant.
source: The current study includes five patients who underwent liver transplant before the era of direct-acting antivirals (DAA) and were viremic at the time of transplant.
evidence: This describes the patient population in the study.

claim: With the advent of DAA therapy, many patients are treated successfully for HCV before liver transplantation.
source: With the advent of DAA therapy, many patients are treated successfully for HCV before liver transplantation (Belli et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The finding of viral steady state during anhepatic phase in the majority of patients and the rapid uptake of HCV by the liver during reperfusion reinforces the benefit of achieving viral negativity with DAA therapy prior to transplantation to prevent infection of the graft.
source: Nevertheless, the finding of viral steady state during anhepatic phase in the majority of patients and the rapid uptake of HCV by the liver during reperfusion reinforces the benefit of achieving not only viral negativity but also achieving less than one virus particle in the entire extracellular body fluid (i.e., cure boundary recently used in Etzion et al., 2020), with DAA therapy prior to transplantation to prevent infection of the graft.
evidence: This is a clinical implication inferred from the study findings.

claim: Following the introduction and reperfusion of the donor liver, the viral load declined in a biphasic manner in Cases 1–4 consistent with an extremely fast viral decline (t1/2~ 5 min) that lasted ~14 min post-reperfusion followed by slower decline (HCV t1/2= 67 min).
source: Another novel finding reported herein is that following the introduction and reperfusion of the donor liver, the viral load declined in a biphasic manner (in Cases 1–4) consistent with an extremely fast viral decline (t1/2~ 5 min) that lasted ~14 min post-reperfusion followed by slower decline (HCV t1/2= 67 min).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the patient data and modeling.

claim: The initial rapid decrease post-reperfusion is hypothesized to be due to entrance into and binding of the virus to the new liver.
source: We hypothesize that the initial rapid decrease is due to entrance into and binding of the virus to the new liver reminiscent of the Ganesan et al., 2011, findings in a mouse model for adenovirus clearance 1 min after infusion.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the data and supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Ganesan et al., 2011, found adenovirus clearance 1 min after infusion in a mouse model.
source: We hypothesize that the initial rapid decrease is due to entrance into and binding of the virus to the new liver reminiscent of the Ganesan et al., 2011, findings in a mouse model for adenovirus clearance 1 min after infusion.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited previous study.

claim: The slower decrease (HCV t1/2 of 67 min) likely represents a more physiological (i.e., infectious) uptake rate of virions by the new liver before new virions are likely to be released from infected cells.
source: The slower decrease (i.e., HCV t1/2 of 67 min) likely represents a more physiological (i.e., infectious) uptake rate of virions by the new liver before new virions are likely to be released from infected cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: Previous efforts to measure serum HCV virion clearance have been performed in chronically infected patients receiving antiviral drugs that inhibit viral production.
source: Previous efforts to measure serum HCV virion clearance have been performed in chronically infected patients receiving antiviral drugs that inhibit viral production (Dahari et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The 67 min for HCV t1/2 estimated in the current study is consistent with previous estimates of the HCV t1/2 of 45 min in patients treated with daclatasvir.
source: Interestingly, the 67 min for HCV t1/2 estimated in the current study is consistent with previous estimates of the HCV t1/2 of 45 min in patients treated with a potent inhibitor, daclatasvir, that blocks virus production (Guedj et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison with a previous study supported by citation.

claim: In Cases 1–4, a rapid resurgence of HCV was observed 6 hr post-reperfusion.
source: While in Cases 1–4, a rapid resurgence of HCV was observed 6 hr post-reperfusion, in Case 5, an extremely slow viral decline was observed during the first 4 hr post-reperfusion (Figure 3 and Table 3), followed by a viral plateau (~2.5 log IU/ml) during the subsequent 6 days (Figure 1A and Supplementary file 3, Table S3).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the patient data.

claim: In Case 5, an extremely slow viral decline was observed during the first 4 hr post-reperfusion, followed by a viral plateau (~2.5 log IU/ml) during the subsequent 6 days.
source: While in Cases 1–4, a rapid resurgence of HCV was observed 6 hr post-reperfusion, in Case 5, an extremely slow viral decline was observed during the first 4 hr post-reperfusion (Figure 3 and Table 3), followed by a viral plateau (~2.5 log IU/ml) during the subsequent 6 days (Figure 1A and Supplementary file 3, Table S3).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the patient data.

claim: The viral plateau in Case 5 might be explained by graft dysfunction due to ischemia-reperfusion injury altering HCV binding to its receptors on hepatocytes.
source: This might be explained by graft dysfunction due to ischemia-reperfusion injury altering HCV binding to its receptors on hepatocytes.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed data.

claim: Garcia-Retortillo et al., 2002, previously reported a slow viral decline post-reperfusion (over 6 hr) in 3 (of 20) patients who underwent liver transplantation, where 2 of the 3 patients had a large degree of ischemia-reperfusion injury.
source: We previously reported a slow viral decline post-reperfusion (over 6 hr) in 3 (of 20) patients who underwent liver transplantation, where 2 of the 3 patients had a large degree of ischemia-reperfusion injury (Garcia-Retortillo et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited previous study.

claim: Closure of porto-collateral vessels is not immediate after transplantation and in some patients blood shunting might contribute to a more modest decrease in HCV viral load during reperfusion.
source: In addition, closure of porto-collateral vessels is not immediate after transplantation and in some patients blood shunting might contribute to a more modest decrease in HCV viral load during reperfusion (Navasa et al., 1993).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation.

claim: Dahari et al., 2005, previously observed an extremely slow viral decline post-reperfusion in some patients and predicted the existence of extrahepatic HCV contribution compartment via mathematical modeling.
source: In addition, we previously observed, in some patients, an extremely slow viral decline post-reperfusion and predicted, via mathematical modeling, the existence of extrahepatic HCV contribution compartment (see Table 1 in Dahari et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited previous study.

claim: The extremely slow viral load decline (or plateau) post-reperfusion in Case 5 might be explained by the existence of an extrahepatic (or second) replication compartment.
source: Thus, the extremely slow viral load decline (or plateau) post-reperfusion in Case 5 might also be explained by the existence of an extrahepatic (or second) replication compartment.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed data.

claim: Case 5 had viral resurgence 3 weeks post-liver transplant.
source: Since Case 5 had viral resurgence 3 weeks post-LT (not shown), we cannot rule out that the observed viral plateau of ~2.5 log IU/mL represents viral production from newly infected hepatocytes of the grafted liver with temporary (~3 weeks) extremely limited viral spread.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the patient data.

claim: The observed viral plateau in Case 5 might represent viral production from newly infected hepatocytes of the grafted liver with temporary (~3 weeks) extremely limited viral spread.
source: Since Case 5 had viral resurgence 3 weeks post-LT (not shown), we cannot rule out that the observed viral plateau of ~2.5 log IU/mL represents viral production from newly infected hepatocytes of the grafted liver with temporary (~3 weeks) extremely limited viral spread.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed data.

claim: An individualized (per case) modeling calibration approach was deemed optimal due to the small number (N = 5) of cases.
source: When fitting the models to the viral load data, an individualized (per case) modeling calibration approach of Equation. 3 and 4 with the measured viral data was deemed optimal due to the small number (N = 5) of cases for whom very frequent viral sampling was measured during the anhepatic phase and immediately after graft reperfusion, respectively.
evidence: This explains the methodological choice made in the study.

claim: A population mixed-effects (pME) modeling approach was found inappropriate for this study.
source: A population mixed-effects (pME) modeling approach was found inappropriate for two main reasons.
evidence: This explains the methodological choice made in the study.

claim: The small sample size of N = 5 was insufficient to accurately train a predictive, population mixed-effects model.
source: In general, the small sample size of N = 5 was insufficient to accurately train a predictive, pME model.
evidence: This is a limitation of the study acknowledged by the authors.

claim: It appears unlikely that additional HCV kinetic data can be acquired to explore mixed-effect models since currently patients are treated successfully with DAA before liver transplantation.
source: Furthermore, it appears unlikely that additional HCV kinetic data can be acquired to explore mixed-effect models since currently patients are treated successfully with DAA before liver transplantation (Feld et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference about future research possibilities supported by a citation.

claim: The cell culture experiments support the notion that hepatocytes not only produce the virus, but also may play a role in clearing the virus from the extracellular space even if the cells are already chronically infected.
source: In the absence of confounding different cell types, our cell culture experiments support the notion that hepatocytes not only produce the virus, but also may play a role in clearing the virus from the extracellular space even if the cells are already chronically infected.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro experimental data.

claim: The t1/2 of HCV in vitro was significantly shorter in the presence of Huh7 cells that were pharmacologically inhibited from secreting virus compared to in the absence of cells.
source: Reminiscent of what was observed in vivo, the t1/2 of HCV in vitro was significantly shorter in the presence of Huh7 cells that were pharmacologically inhibited from secreting virus compared to in the absence of cells.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the in vitro experiments.

claim: Daclatasvir at 1 nM effectively blocks de novo virus secretion.
source: We used chronically infected cells to avoid any initial rapid binding and influx of HCV as would be expected if naïve Huh7 cells were introduced and utilized the well-characterized drugs daclatasvir or naringenin at doses known to effectively block de novo virus secretion (Goldwasser et al., 2011; Hu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Naringenin at 200 µM effectively blocks de novo virus secretion.
source: We used chronically infected cells to avoid any initial rapid binding and influx of HCV as would be expected if naïve Huh7 cells were introduced and utilized the well-characterized drugs daclatasvir or naringenin at doses known to effectively block de novo virus secretion (Goldwasser et al., 2011; Hu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Neither daclatasvir nor naringenin are known to enhance the degradation rate of HCV particles in the media.
source: Because neither daclatasvir nor naringenin are known to enhance the degradation rate of HCV particles in the media, the data suggest that a large amount of the virus in the media enters and/or binds to the cells over time.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about these drugs.

claim: A large amount of the virus in the media enters and/or binds to the cells over time in the in vitro experiments.
source: Because neither daclatasvir nor naringenin are known to enhance the degradation rate of HCV particles in the media, the data suggest that a large amount of the virus in the media enters and/or binds to the cells over time.
evidence: This is inferred from the in vitro experimental results.

claim: The HCV t½ measured in the presence of cells in vitro may be overestimated if daclatasvir or naringenin do not completely block HCVcc secretion.
source: Of note, the HCV t½ measured in the presence of cells in vitro may be overestimated if daclatasvir or naringenin do not completely block cell culture produced HCV (HCVcc) secretion, hence the difference in HCV t1/2 calculated compared to the absence of cells may be underestimated.
evidence: This is a caveat about the interpretation of the in vitro data.

claim: Hepatoma cells in vitro and the HCVcc virions they produce are not identical to in vivo infection.
source: While we find this in vitro data interesting, it is important to note that hepatoma cells in vitro and the HCVcc virions they produce are not identical to in vivo infection and thus more investigation is needed before specific conclusions can be drawn directly from the in vitro data.
evidence: This is a limitation of the in vitro model acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The vast majority of HCV RNA in the culture media in vitro is non-infectious (e.g., specific infectivity of 1:500–1:1000).
source: Because the vast majority of HCV RNA in the culture media in vitro is non-infectious (e.g., specific infectivity of 1:500–1:1000) (Wakita et al., 2005; Cai et al., 2005; Hueging et al., 2015; Sarhan et al., 2017) and superinfection exclusion has been reported (Schaller et al., 2007), we assume this entry is primarily non-productive.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Superinfection exclusion has been reported for HCV.
source: Because the vast majority of HCV RNA in the culture media in vitro is non-infectious (e.g., specific infectivity of 1:500–1:1000) (Wakita et al., 2005; Cai et al., 2005; Hueging et al., 2015; Sarhan et al., 2017) and superinfection exclusion has been reported (Schaller et al., 2007), we assume this entry is primarily non-productive.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The entry of HCV into chronically infected cells in vitro is assumed to be primarily non-productive.
source: Because the vast majority of HCV RNA in the culture media in vitro is non-infectious (e.g., specific infectivity of 1:500–1:1000) (Wakita et al., 2005; Cai et al., 2005; Hueging et al., 2015; Sarhan et al., 2017) and superinfection exclusion has been reported (Schaller et al., 2007), we assume this entry is primarily non-productive.
evidence: This is an assumption based on cited previous studies.

claim: Whether the non-productive uptake of HCV involves an HCV-specific entry mechanism or represents some sort of general supernatant sampling remains to be determined.
source: However, whether this non-productive uptake involves an HCV-specific entry mechanism (i.e., involves HCV receptors) or represents some sort of general supernatant sampling, by which the hepatoma cells may be acquiring nutrients or clearing debris remains to be determined.
evidence: This identifies an open question for future research.

claim: Questions regarding the relative contribution of different cells in the liver to the observed HCV clearance in patients will likely require the use of in vivo models of HCV infection.
source: However, because it is suspect to extrapolate quantitative differences in cell behavior from cell culture to the in vivo situation, questions regarding the relative contribution of the different cells in the liver to the observed HCV clearance in patients will likely require the use of in vivo models of HCV infection, such as urokinase-type plasminogen activator/severe combined immunodeficiency mice transplanted with human hepatocytes (Uchida et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research based on the limitations of the current study.

claim: The current data raises the possibility that hepatocytes might be involved in HCV clearance.
source: The current data simply raises the possibility that hepatocytes might be involved and helps justify the further investigation of this hypothesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study data.

claim: Others have suggested hepatic involvement in the clearing of simian immunodeficiency virus and adenovirus in animals.
source: Others have suggested hepatic involvement in the clearing of simian immunodeficiency virus and adenovirus in animals (Ganesan et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The current study is the first one to investigate hepatocyte involvement in viral clearance in vitro.
source: However, to our best knowledge, the current study is the first one to investigate this in vitro, providing evidence that hepatocytes may contribute to viral clearance, but it remains to be determined the extent to which hepatocytes contribute to HCV clearance and if the involvement of hepatocytes might be different for non-hepatotropic viruses.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current study.

claim: It remains to be determined the extent to which hepatocytes contribute to HCV clearance.
source: However, to our best knowledge, the current study is the first one to investigate this in vitro, providing evidence that hepatocytes may contribute to viral clearance, but it remains to be determined the extent to which hepatocytes contribute to HCV clearance and if the involvement of hepatocytes might be different for non-hepatotropic viruses.
evidence: This identifies an open question for future research.

claim: It remains to be determined if the involvement of hepatocytes in viral clearance might be different for non-hepatotropic viruses.
source: However, to our best knowledge, the current study is the first one to investigate this in vitro, providing evidence that hepatocytes may contribute to viral clearance, but it remains to be determined the extent to which hepatocytes contribute to HCV clearance and if the involvement of hepatocytes might be different for non-hepatotropic viruses.
evidence: This identifies an open question for future research.

claim: Five transplant recipients with median age 60 years (range, 49–68) and median BMI 30 kg/m2 (range, 19–34) underwent liver transplantation.
source: Five transplant recipients (termed cases) with median age 60 years (range, 49–68) and median BMI 30 kg/m2 (range, 19–34) underwent liver transplantation (Table 1).
evidence: This describes the patient population in the study.

claim: Four of the five liver donors were male with median age 69 years (range, 29–73).
source: Four of the five liver donors were male with median age 69 years (range, 29–73) (Table 1).
evidence: This describes the donor population in the study.

claim: All patients received 500 mg methylprednisolone immediately before laparotomy and 500 mg during graft reperfusion.
source: All patients received 500 mg methylprednisolone immediately before laparotomy and 500 mg during graft reperfusion.
evidence: This describes the treatment protocol used in the study.

claim: Blood samples (2 mL) were taken before liver transplantation, every 5–15 min during the anhepatic phase for a total of 7–12 samples, every 5 min during the first hour of reperfusion, and every 10 min until the end of surgery for a total of 15–21 samples.
source: For each patient, blood samples (2 mL) were taken before liver transplantation, every 5–15 min during the anhepatic phase for a total of 7–12 samples, every 5 min during the first hour of reperfusion, and every 10 min until the end of surgery for a total of 15–21 samples.
evidence: This describes the sampling protocol used in the study.

claim: Blood was sampled every hour for the first 6 hr after surgery, every 6 hr during the first day, and daily during the first week.
source: Thereafter, blood was sampled every hour for the first 6 hr, every 6 hr during the first day, and daily during the first week.
evidence: This describes the sampling protocol used in the study.

claim: Transfusion of blood products, saline, and albumin were recorded.
source: Transfusion of blood products, saline, and albumin were recorded.
evidence: This describes data collection during the study.

claim: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee at Hospital Clinic Barcelona and all patients provided a written informed consent.
source: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee at Hospital Clinic Barcelona and all patients provided a written informed consent.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: Shortly before liver removal, virus is assumed to be produced at constant rate P and cleared from the serum at rate c per virion.
source: Shortly before liver removal, we assume that virus is produced at constant rate P and cleared from the serum at rate c per virion as in Neumann et al., 1998
evidence: This is a modeling assumption supported by a citation.

claim: During the anhepatic phase and 4 hr after reperfusion, virus production is assumed to cease (P = 0).
source: During the anhepatic phase and 4 hr after reperfusion, we assume that in the absence of the liver (i.e., anhepatic phase), virus production ceases, P = 0.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption based on biological reasoning.

claim: Blood loss causes a reduction in the absolute amount of virus in circulation, but does not affect the virus concentration.
source: The blood loss causes a reduction in the absolute amount of virus in circulation, but does not affect the virus concentration, V.
evidence: This is a modeling consideration based on mathematical reasoning.

claim: Fluid intake results in a dilution of viral concentration.
source: In contrast, the fluid intake results in a dilution of V.
evidence: This is a modeling consideration based on mathematical reasoning.

claim: The total fluid volume before surgery, F(0), was calculated using the patient's body weight under the assumption of 15 L of extracellular fluid per 70 kg.
source: Therefore, the total fluid volume before surgery, F(0), was calculated using the patient's body weight (Table 1) under the assumption of 15 L of extracellular fluid per 70 kg.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption used in the analysis.

claim: The study explored utilizing just 5 L of blood per 70 kg as an alternative assumption.
source: In addition, we explored utilizing just 5 L of blood per 70 kg since transfusions are mainly given to compensate for blood loss during transplantation and HCV viral load is typically higher by several orders of magnitude in the blood compared to the other diverse body fluids (Numata et al., 1993; Pfaender et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes an alternative modeling approach explored in the study.

claim: HCV viral load is typically higher by several orders of magnitude in the blood compared to other diverse body fluids.
source: In addition, we explored utilizing just 5 L of blood per 70 kg since transfusions are mainly given to compensate for blood loss during transplantation and HCV viral load is typically higher by several orders of magnitude in the blood compared to the other diverse body fluids (Numata et al., 1993; Pfaender et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Model calibration was performed using Python 3.7.4 together with Scipy Version 1.3.1 and Numpy Version 1.17.2.
source: Model calibration was performed using Python 3.7.4 together with Scipy Version 1.3.1 and Numpy Version 1.17.2.
evidence: This describes the computational tools used in the study.

source: The fitting used the optimize.least_squares function in Scipy, which minimizes the squares of the differences between the model and patient data (least squares).
evidence: This describes the computational method used in the study.

claim: Results with p-values ≤ 0.05 were considered statistically significant.
source: Results with p-values ≤ 0.05 were considered statistically significant.
evidence: This describes the statistical threshold used in the study.

source: The viral slope was considered flat (or plateau) if the estimate was not significantly different from 0, that is, p > 0.05.
evidence: This describes the statistical criterion used in the study.

claim: Huh7 human hepatoma cells were obtained from the Japanese Collection of Research Bioresources Cell Bank.
source: Huh7 human hepatoma cells (JCRB0403; RRID.CVCL_0336) were obtained from the Japanese Collection of Research Bioresources Cell Bank.

claim: Cell stocks have only been passaged 19 times.
source: Cell stocks have only been passaged 19 times.
evidence: This describes the cell culture protocol used in the study.

claim: Every time a new stock is generated, cells are mycoplasma-tested prior to freezing.
source: Every time a new stock is generated, cells are mycoplasma-tested prior to freezing.
evidence: This describes the quality control protocol used in the study.

claim: Stocks of HCVcc were generated from a plasmid encoding the JFH-1 genome that was provided by Takaji Wakita.
source: Stocks of HCVcc were generated as previously described from a plasmid encoding the JFH-1 genome that was provided by Takaji Wakita (National Institute of Infectious Diseases, Tokyo, Japan) (Zhong et al., 2005; Yu and Uprichard, 2010; Wakita et al., 2005).
evidence: This describes the source of materials used in the study.

claim: To measure the HCVcc half-life in the absence of cells, the JFH-1 HCVcc stock was diluted to 104 ffU/mL.
source: To measure the HCVcc half-life in the absence of cells, the JFH-1 HCVcc stock was diluted to 104 ffU/mL, which is the level observed in culture media during steady state in the JFH-1 HCVcc infection system (Zhong et al., 2005) and incubated at 37°C simulating conditions during HCV infection in cell culture.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used in the study.

claim: 104 ffU/mL is the level observed in culture media during steady state in the JFH-1 HCVcc infection system.
source: To measure the HCVcc half-life in the absence of cells, the JFH-1 HCVcc stock was diluted to 104 ffU/mL, which is the level observed in culture media during steady state in the JFH-1 HCVcc infection system (Zhong et al., 2005) and incubated at 37°C simulating conditions during HCV infection in cell culture.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: To measure HCVcc half-life in the presence of chronically HCV-infected cells, confluent non-growing Huh7 cells were infected with JFH-1 HCVcc at a low MOI (0.01) and cultured for 12 days until HCV levels reached a steady state.
source: To measure HCVcc half-life in the presence of chronically HCV-infected cells, confluent non-growing Huh7 cells (~60,000 cells/well) (Yu and Uprichard, 2010) were infected with JFH-1 HCVcc at a low MOI (0.01) and cultured for 12 days until HCV levels reached a steady state.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used in the study.

claim: Cells were treated with 1 nM daclatasvir to stop HCV replication and infectious virus secretion (a dose 36 times the reported EC50).
source: Cells were then treated with 1 nM daclatasvir (provided by Bristol-Myers Squibb, NYC, NY) to stop HCV replication and infectious virus secretion (a dose 36 times the reported EC50 [19]) or 200 μM naringenin to block HCV secretion (a dose reported to block 74% of JFH-1 HCVcc secretion; Goldwasser et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used in the study.

claim: 200 μM naringenin is a dose reported to block 74% of JFH-1 HCVcc secretion.
source: Cells were then treated with 1 nM daclatasvir (provided by Bristol-Myers Squibb, NYC, NY) to stop HCV replication and infectious virus secretion (a dose 36 times the reported EC50 [19]) or 200 μM naringenin to block HCV secretion (a dose reported to block 74% of JFH-1 HCVcc secretion; Goldwasser et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Mouse liver RNA was added as an internal extraction efficiency control.
source: Mouse liver RNA was added as an internal extraction efficiency control and total RNA was isolated using an ABI PRISM 6100 Nucleic Acid Prepstation (Applied Biosystems), using the manufacturer's instructions.
